report.source_text: Native T1-mapping demonstrated markedly elevated T1 values with preponderance in the inferoseptal wall (1068 ± 73 ms in the entire slice vs. 1122 ± 31 ms in the inferoseptal wall), also see Figs. 1a and 2a. Furthermore, T2-mapping revealed increased values (entire slice 52 ± 6 ms, inferoseptal wall 55 ± 6 ms), suggesting myocardial edema representing active myocardial inflammation by hantavirus infection. In contrast, the LGE image, potentially indicating irreversible myocardial damage if positive, in the corresponding slice was negative (Fig. 1c).

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 36-year-old male presented with headache and abdominal pain, along with signs of hantavirus infection including thrombocytopenia, elevated creatinine, proteinuria, and positive Puumala virus serology. Initial ECG showed sinus rhythm with T-wave inversion and incomplete RBBB. Six days later, he developed chest pain and dyspnea, accompanied by elevated high sensitivity troponin I and creatinkinase. Coronary artery disease was ruled out by coronary CT angiography after creatinine normalized. Cardiac Magnetic Resonance (CMR) imaging revealed markedly elevated native T1- and T2-mapping values, suggesting myocardial edema and active inflammation, despite negative late gadolinium enhancement (LGE). Based on clinical symptoms, increased cardiac biomarkers, exclusion of CAD, and conspicuous native T1- and T2-mapping values on CMR, a diagnosis of hantavirus-induced myocarditis was made.
